page.title: Live Event Production Webinar: Decisions, Roles, and Run of Show
page.description: A practical guide to the first decisions, crew roles, rehearsal plan, and escalation steps for producing a live webinar on any platform.
page.h1: What should you decide first about live event production webinar?
page.definition: A live event production webinar is a planned, crewed broadcast delivered on a streaming platform where a producer owns the run of show, rehearses speakers, manages a backup stream, and handles real-time issues so the host can focus on content.
page.quick_answer: Lock the platform, assign a single producer to own the run of show, schedule one full rehearsal on the real platform two to five days before, and confirm a backup stream before you announce the date.

sections.h2: Which platform choice drives the rest of the production plan?

blocks.p: Pick the platform before you finalize the agenda because the feature set determines rehearsal needs, backup options, and crew roles. Self-serve studios such as StreamYard or Livestorm suit simple webinars; enterprise suites such as ON24, Cvent, Bizzabo, or Goldcast add registration, analytics, and breakout rooms but require longer setup. Ten platforms compared below, from self-serve streaming studios to enterprise event suites.

sections.h2: Who owns the run of show and what does that document include?

blocks.p: One producer owns the run of show from intake through publishing. The document lists every cue, speaker name, slide deck version, lower-third text, video roll-in, poll launch time, and contingency trigger. It is the single source of truth for the platform operator, moderator, and speaker manager.

ul: Slide deck file name and version

sections.h2: What rehearsal cadence prevents live failures?

blocks.p: Schedule one full rehearsal on the real platform two to five days before the event, plus a technical check sixty minutes before going live. The full rehearsal runs every transition, tests the backup stream switch, and confirms each speaker's audio, camera, and screen share. The technical check verifies encoder health, internet stability, and that the latest slide deck is loaded.

ol: Full rehearsal: two to five days prior, all speakers, producer, moderator, platform operator
Technical check: sixty minutes prior, producer and platform operator only
Go-live huddle: five minutes prior, confirm run of show version and escalation contacts

sections.h2: How do you staff a webinar versus a summit or hybrid event?

blocks.p: A simple webinar needs one producer who also operates the platform and moderates Q&A. Summits and hybrid events require a show caller, speaker manager, moderator, and dedicated platform operator. Eight workstreams, each with one owner, keep the plan from collapsing when issues arise.

sections.h2: What escalation plan covers unrehearsed speakers and technical failure?

blocks.p: Define three escalation levels before the event: speaker issue, platform issue, and full failover. For unrehearsed speakers, the speaker manager holds a private chat channel and can mute or replace the feed within thirty seconds. For platform failure, the producer triggers the backup stream on a second encoder and posts a holding slide with a one-sentence message. Document the decision tree and share it with every crew member.

ul: Level one: speaker audio or video drops, speaker manager intervenes via back channel
Level two: platform feature fails (polls, Q&A), moderator switches to manual process
Level three: primary stream dies, producer cuts to backup stream and posts holding slide

sections.h2: What deliverables should you expect from a production partner?

blocks.p: A production partner delivers the run of show, speaker brief and rehearsal, branded slide template and lower thirds, live producer, Q&A moderation, backup stream, edited recording, and short clips for social. West Peek Productions produces virtual, hybrid and webinar events and sets up marketing, content and creative operations; it does not sell event software. Moderated webinars range from two thousand five hundred to seven thousand five hundred dollars per production; executive summits, online conferences and hybrid productions range from ten thousand to fifty thousand dollars and above. Platform and production are two purchases: the platform is software; production is the crew, cameras, encoder, run of show and backup stream.

ul: Branded slide template and lower thirds
Edited recording delivered within twenty-four to forty-eight hours

faq.q: How far in advance should I book a production partner for a webinar?
faq.a: Allow three to four weeks from brief to live for a single webinar; a repeat format can move faster. For a summit or online conference, plan six to eight weeks of management lead time.

faq.q: Can I use my existing Zoom Webinars or Teams license with a production crew?
faq.a: Yes. Production crews work on the platform you already use, such as Zoom Webinars, Microsoft Teams, ON24, or StreamYard. The crew brings the run of show, backup encoder, and live operations; you keep the platform contract.

faq.q: What is the difference between a platform fee and a production fee?
faq.a: The platform fee covers software access and attendee capacity. The production fee covers the producer, speaker manager, platform operator, backup stream, rehearsal time, and post-event editing. They are separate line items from separate vendors.

faq.q: Do I need a backup stream for a simple webinar?
faq.a: Yes. A backup stream on a second encoder protects against primary internet or encoder failure. The producer monitors both and can cut over in seconds with a holding slide so attendees never see a blank screen.

faq.q: How quickly should the replay and clips be delivered?
faq.a: Send the replay within twenty-four to forty-eight hours while attendees still remember the event. Short clips for social perform best when posted the same week.
